conceptTag: Did the campaign cause the sales?
readerTitle: The flyer went out, and sales jumped. Was it the flyer?
caseNote: 가상 사례 (철물점 체인, 포장재 제조사) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 캠페인은 보통 잘 팔릴 시기에 맞춰 나가기 때문에, 매출 상승과 캠페인이 함께 움직이는 것은 처음부터 정해진 일이다. 효과를 알려면 캠페인을 받지 않은 비교 집단이 필요하다.
misconception: 캠페인 직후 매출이 올랐으면 캠페인 덕분이다. 작년보다 더 올랐으면 그 차이만큼이 캠페인 효과다.

sources.text: 통계와 실험 설계의 표준 개념 (상관과 인과, 교란 변수, 무작위 대조군·홀드아웃)

factChecks.note: 모든 수치는 설명용 가상 수치입니다. 계산: 올해 3월→4월 +22%, 작년 같은 기간(전단지 없음) +18%, 차이 22 − 18 = 4%포인트. 카드에서는 '4 points'로 적어 상대 비율과 혼동하지 않게 했습니다.
포장재 사례: 유통사 300곳 중 무작위 150곳에만 리베이트 제안. 수치는 가상이며 리베이트 비율(5%)도 설명용입니다.
이 레슨은 apply 레슨으로 새 개념을 도입하지 않습니다. 사용한 개념: THK-08-01(상관≠인과), THK-08-06(통제 실험). 선택 편향(THK-08-04)은 설문 레슨(THK-08-08)과 겹치지 않도록 언급만 피했습니다.

cards.title: The flyer went out, and sales jumped. Was it the flyer?
body: You run a chain of eight hardware stores. In early April you mail a discount flyer to every neighborhood you serve.
April sales come in 22% higher than March. Your marketing lead wants to double the flyer budget for May. Before you sign, it's worth asking what else happens in April.

image.label: Hardware store shelves with garden tools and a flyer on the counter
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 동네 철물점 계산대 위에 할인 전단지 한 장, 뒤편 선반에는 봄 원예용품(화분, 호스, 씨앗 봉투)이 가득. 창밖에 꽃이 핀 나무. 실제 브랜드 로고 없음.

cards.title: What's your first read on the 22%?
body: The flyer cost real money, and the team is excited. You want to know how much of the jump the flyer actually caused.

options.text: Credit the flyer. Sales rose right after it went out
options.feedback: Fast and motivating, but timing alone only shows the two moved together. That's **correlation, not causation**: spring may have lifted sales with or without the flyer.

options.text: Compare with last year's March-to-April change, when there was no flyer
options.feedback: This separates the season from the flyer. It's still not proof, since other things changed since last year, but it removes the biggest rival explanation.

options.text: Ask customers at checkout whether they saw the flyer
options.feedback: You learn who noticed it, not who came because of it. Loyal regulars read flyers and shop in spring anyway, so this is still a correlation.

cards.title: Most of the jump was already coming.
body: Spring is gardening and repair season. Last year April beat March by 18% with no flyer at all. That leaves **4 points** the flyer *might* explain, and even those could be weather or a competitor's closure.

breakdown.label: Left to explain
breakdown.detail: The most the flyer could take credit for

cards.title: The season caused both.
body: Here's the trap. You mailed the flyer in April *because* April is busy. The same thing, a rising season, pushed both the campaign and the sales.
That is **correlation is not causation** in its most common business form. Campaigns are timed for good weeks, so they almost always look like they worked.
Comparing to last year helps. But a fair answer needs stores that went through the same April without the flyer.

cards.title: Next time, hold some stores back.
body: For May, mail the flyer around four stores and skip the other four. Same weeks, same weather, same economy. The only planned difference is the flyer.
This is a **controlled experiment**. The group without the campaign, often called a *holdout*, shows what would have happened anyway. The gap between the groups is the flyer's effect.

image.label: Eight stores split into two groups, one with flyers
image.brief: 지도 위 상점 아이콘 8개를 두 줄로 나눔. 위쪽 4개 주변에만 전단지 아이콘, 아래쪽 4개는 비어 있음. 각 그룹 옆에 막대그래프, 두 막대 사이 간격에 'Flyer effect' 라벨.

cards.softwareNote: Digital teams do this with a holdout: a random slice of users, often 5–10%, never gets the email or push campaign. Without it, a campaign sent in a busy week looks like a success every time.

cards.title: Which four stores get the flyer?
body: Your stores differ in size and neighborhood. How do you pick the four that get the May flyer?

options.text: The four strongest stores, where the flyer will have the most impact
options.feedback: Those stores would outsell the others anyway, so the test credits the flyer for their strength. The groups must start alike, or the **experiment** measures the stores, not the flyer.

options.text: Pair stores of similar size, then flip a coin within each pair
options.feedback: Matching keeps the groups alike, and the coin keeps your hopes out of the choice. It costs a little planning and buys a result you can trust.
Easy to run and builds buy-in. But eager managers may also push harder on the floor, so their stores could win for reasons other than the flyer.

cards.title: Holdouts have costs and limits.
body: Holding back means giving up some sales in the holdout stores if the flyer does work. Keep the test short and the holdout as small as still gives a clear answer.
Eight stores is a small test. One month may show noise, not effect, so repeat it before betting big. And some effects arrive late: a flyer can bring a customer back in June.

cards.title: Now it's a packaging manufacturer.
body: You make cardboard boxes and sell through 300 distributors. Last autumn you offered every distributor a 5% volume rebate, and fourth-quarter orders hit a record.
Sales wants to repeat the rebate this autumn. How do you find out if it actually works?

options.text: Run it for everyone again and compare with last year's record
options.feedback: Better than nothing, but autumn is peak shipping season for boxes. A year-on-year comparison still mixes the rebate with the economy and your customers' own growth.

options.text: Offer it to a random 150 distributors, compare orders with the other 150
options.feedback: This is a **controlled experiment**: same season, same market, one difference. The cost is managing distributors who notice they weren't offered the deal.

options.text: Offer it only to the distributors who ordered most last autumn
options.feedback: They're your biggest buyers in peak season anyway. Their orders will rise, and you'll mistake their size for the rebate's effect: **correlation, not causation**.

cards.title: A campaign's effect is the gap to a group that didn't get it.
body: **Concepts used:** *Correlation is not causation* (campaigns are timed for busy weeks, so sales rise with them anyway) and *Controlled experiments* (a fair holdout shows what would have happened without the campaign).
**Try it today:** pick your last promotion. Write down what else changed in the same weeks. Then plan which customers or locations you'd hold back next time.
